title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: a single blade of grass that fire cannot burn and wind cannot lift

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakti as a philosophy through one verse: Shiva joined with Shakti is able to create, and without her he cannot even stir. Did you give one stalled thing a stir? Day one thousand eighty-three.

The gods have just won a victory, and they are very pleased with themselves. That's where a short scene in the Kena Upanishad begins. Then something appears in front of them that they don't recognize: a mysterious being, a yaksha. Agni, the god of fire, goes up to it, boasting that he can burn anything on earth. The being sets down one blade of grass and says: burn this. Agni throws everything he has at it. The grass doesn't even scorch. Then Vayu, the wind, who says he can carry off anything at all. He can't lift the blade of grass an inch. Two gods, two powers, one straw. Today: who finally tells them what they were looking at.
screen: `THE GODS ARE PROUD.` → `ONE BLADE OF GRASS.` → `FIRE CAN'T BURN IT. WIND CAN'T LIFT IT.`

segments.voice: Next the gods send Indra, their king. He walks toward the being, and it vanishes. And right there, in that same space, he meets a woman, radiant and beautifully adorned: Uma, the daughter of the Himalaya. He asks her: what was that? She tells him. That was Brahman, the ultimate reality. Your victory was its victory, and you took the credit. Turn it the first way: the lesson about power. Fire could burn because something greater let it burn. Wind could blow because something greater let it blow. Take that away, and even a blade of grass is too heavy. The gods' powers were real, but they were borrowed. Turn it a second way: who explains it. In this Upanishad, the one who knows, the one who can name Brahman to the king of the gods, is Uma, a woman of the mountains. Later tradition knows Uma as a name of Parvati, Shiva's wife. Some who worship the goddess point to this scene: when the gods are lost, Shakti is the teacher who stands in the empty place and speaks. A third way: where she appears. The being vanishes, and she is there in the very same space. Some readers hear that as the heart of the idea. Brahman is beyond sight, beyond fire and wind. Shakti is the side of that reality that turns toward you, the face that answers. A fourth way, and the plainest. The scene begins with pride and ends with a question. Indra doesn't win anything here. He just asks, and listens. The Upanishad says that Agni, Vayu and Indra came to stand above the other gods because they came closest to Brahman, and Indra above them because he was the first to know it.
screen: `THE BEING VANISHES. UMA IS THERE.` · `THE GODS' POWERS WERE BORROWED.` · `UMA IS THE ONE WHO KNOWS.` · `SHE STANDS IN THE EMPTY PLACE.` · then, large: `THAT WAS BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay where it vanished. Sit and let the breath settle. Watch for the moment a thought ends: a plan finishes, a memory fades, a sound outside stops. Don't rush to the next one. Stay in that small empty place for a breath or two, the way Indra stayed where the being disappeared. Something else will arrive. Let it, and wait for the next ending. If you pray, you can hold the name of the goddess, or the name you use for God, in that empty place. If you don't, just keep waiting there. The bell holds the time.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Kena Upanishad, fire and wind fail before one blade of grass, and Uma stands where the mystery vanished and names it Brahman.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Today, at one moment when you're sure you already know the answer, ask one real question instead, the way Indra did. Day one thousand eighty-three.

howItsDone: The Kena Upanishad is studied in Vedanta schools, and the scene of Uma explaining Brahman to Indra is retold in talks on the goddess.

original.note: Sanskrit: Uma, the goddess who explains Brahman to Indra in the Kena Upanishad; a name of Parvati.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about which god is strongest.
what it means: every power the gods had was borrowed, and Uma is the one who tells them so.
what a scholar hears: Kena Upanishad 3.12, umāṃ haimavatīm: Uma, daughter of Himavat, appears in the very space where the yaksha vanished.
recall: the year just walked and kept

notes: Kena 3.1–4.3 paraphrased: the gods' victory, the yaksha, Agni and the grass (tṛṇam), Vayu, Indra, Uma Haimavati 'bahu-śobhamānā', her answer 'brahma', and 4.2–4.3 on Agni, Vayu and Indra standing above the other gods, Indra as the first to know it. Confirm the paraphrase, especially 'the first to know it' (prathamo vidāṃcakāra).
'Uma is the name later stories give to Parvati' and 'people who worship the goddess often point to this scene': a historical and a 'often' claim; Keeper to confirm or soften to 'some'.
Reading of Uma as Shakti, the face of Brahman that answers, is attributed to 'some readers'.
